question: Can simple stochastic-process summaries of thresholded hidden-unit activations distinguish image classifiers trained to generalize from classifiers trained on randomized labels to memorize, without requiring a held-out test set?

key_findings.claim: Across the displayed experiments, randomized-label training is usually associated with a lower mean last-hidden-layer activation rate than ordinary training, but the separation is conditional on architecture, width, which layers are trainable, and how much of the random-label dataset is actually fitted.
key_findings.evidence: For the 64-unit MNIST MLP, Table 2 reports train-set MFR 0.62 for the generalizing model versus 0.03 for MemRetrainLast and 0.12 for MemRandomLast; for the 64-unit CIFAR-10 DenseNet, the corresponding values are 0.49, 0.03, and 0.04. The all-layers DenseNet condition is much closer to the generalizing/random states (0.43 versus 0.49/0.53), and Figures 3-4 show overlap increasing with width. Table 1 also shows that several models called memorizing fit only 17.31%-63.80% of randomized training labels, so the contrast is not uniformly between a generalizer and a fully memorizing network.

key_findings.claim: The paper's Poisson interpretation is contradicted by its own construction and Figure 6: thresholding one activation per input creates Bernoulli trials, whose finite-window count is binomial with Fano factor 1-p, not Poisson with Fano factor 1.
key_findings.evidence: The method maps every unit/sample pair to exactly 0 or 1 and uses activation frequency as lambda. For independent identically distributed inputs, a window of w such observations has mean wp and variance wp(1-p), hence Fano factor 1-p. The reported mean Fano factors track approximately one minus MFR throughout Tables 2 and 5 (for example, Dense-64 MNIST generalizing MFR 0.62 and mean Fano 0.38; random MFR 0.45 and mean Fano 0.55), and Figure 6 displays the resulting near-perfect inverse line. Thus the reported underdispersion is the expected Bernoulli/binomial identity at these non-rare firing probabilities, not merely an unexplained defect of an otherwise supported Poisson model.

key_findings.claim: The stochastic-process exposition contains multiple malformed equations, weakening the manuscript as a mathematical formulation independently of the empirical results.
key_findings.evidence: The Poisson mass function on page 3 divides by n rather than n!, so it is not normalized. The exponential density is written as the point probability P(T=t), the Erlang expression uses the undefined denominator (n-1)! instead of (k-1)!, and the mean-ergodicity example omits a time-average normalization while integrating X_t with respect to x over an infinite range. The source TeX confirms these are manuscript expressions rather than extraction artifacts.

anchors.section: 2.1 / stationarity, ergodicity, and Poisson Process equations

key_findings.claim: The claimed evidence for independence, stationarity, and train/test distributional similarity is not auditable and does not establish the asserted properties.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports Ljung-Box tests with combined p-values and Augmented Dickey-Fuller tests but gives no lag choices, per-node or aggregate statistics, p-values, rejection counts, or code. ADF non-rejection/rejection behavior on binary activations is not a general stationarity test. Table 2 marks KS p-values above a threshold as significant similarities, even though failure to reject equality is not an equivalence test; moreover 0.05/128 is 0.000390625, not the caption's 0.00027. Therefore the conclusion that training and test activations do not differ, and hence that an external test set is unnecessary, is materially stronger than the presented statistics support.

key_findings.claim: Mean firing rate changes rapidly when training switches from true labels to randomized labels and then appears broadly stable in the displayed pooled curves, but this is an exploratory trace rather than a validated early-warning criterion.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 follows ten epochs of ordinary training with 100 epochs on randomized labels and estimates MFR from 100 samples after every batch. Both panels show a sharp transition and later plateau; the all-layers CIFAR-10 trace is a stated exception with a continuing rise. The plot groups results by dataset with confidence bands but reports no seed count, run-level variability, detection threshold, lead time, false-positive rate, or comparison against validation-based early stopping.

key_findings.claim: The experiment varies five model states across three datasets and multiple widths, yet its design cannot isolate memorization from optimization progress, parameter movement, sparsity, model capacity, or the location of trainable layers.
key_findings.evidence: The randomized-label conditions start either from trained or random weights, freeze either all but the last two layers or no layers, and reach sharply different training accuracies. All runs use SGD at learning rate 0.1 with no momentum, but epochs, stopping criteria, random seeds, grid-search space, label-shuffle realization, and run counts are not reported. ReLU activation frequency is sensitive to biases and parameter scaling, so lower MFR cannot be attributed uniquely to memorization in this factorially incomplete comparison.

key_findings.claim: The public research artifact supports manuscript inspection but not computational reproduction.
key_findings.evidence: The exact arXiv v1 source archive (SHA-256 25bbe4eb71ff47ee69ce01c6111ed2686358b7b7eae05fdc5206cf53fdd62354) contains TeX, bibliographies, 36 plot/image assets, and style/template files, but no experiment code, notebooks, raw tables, checkpoints, environment lock, or result traces. The appendix lists package and workstation versions, with ambiguous package labels such as 'Neocore', 'Statsmodel', and 'Scipy.Stats', but supplies no executable setup. No code URL appears in the paper or source, and exact-title/author GitHub repository searches returned no official experiment repository as of the review date.

method.core_idea: Treat the sequence of positive-versus-nonpositive activations of each unit as a spike train, summarize the last hidden layer using firing-rate and Fano-factor statistics, and compare those summaries across random, ordinary-training, and randomized-label-training states.
method.mechanism: MLPs and one-layer CNNs are trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, while ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121 features feed a variable-width ReLU layer for CIFAR-10. Hidden widths are 64, 128, 256, and 512. The paper contrasts an untrained random network, an ordinarily trained network, retraining of the last two layers on shuffled labels, training the last two layers from a random network on shuffled labels, and all-layer retraining on shuffled labels. Each last-hidden-layer activation is thresholded at zero; per-unit positive fractions, windowed Fano factors, their layer means, and coefficients of variation are analyzed with KS, Ljung-Box, combined-p-value, and ADF procedures and tracked during a true-label-to-shuffled-label training transition.
assumptions: Sample order can be treated as discrete time for a stochastic activation process.
Thresholding at zero retains the information needed to distinguish memorization from generalization across architectures and input scales.
Per-sample activation indicators are adequately described by a homogeneous Poisson arrival process rather than a Bernoulli process.
Randomizing a finite dataset's order makes the indicator sequence sufficiently independent and stationary.
Last-hidden-layer summaries capture the location where memorization is implemented, or deviations can be explained as memorization moving to earlier layers.
Training on shuffled labels operationalizes memorization even when randomized-label training accuracy remains far below 100%.
Non-rejection by KS, Ljung-Box, or ADF procedures supports similarity, independence, or stationarity strongly enough for the paper's conclusions.
Pooling across widths, architectures, datasets, and training states yields meaningful confidence bands despite unreported independent-run counts.

techniques.role: Converts each last-hidden-unit ReLU response into a binary active/inactive indicator using zero as the threshold.
Uses each unit's positive fraction as a firing-rate parameter and averages it across the observed layer.
Computes window-100 count variance divided by count mean for each unit, then summarizes its layer distribution.
Creates deliberately non-generalizing training targets and three retraining/freezing regimes intended to induce memorization.
Applies KS comparisons to firing-rate distributions across model states and train/test splits.
Uses Ljung-Box and ADF procedures as exploratory checks for autocorrelation and unit-root behavior.
Samples 100 inputs after each batch to visualize MFR before and after switching from true to randomized labels.

evaluations.setting: MNIST and FashionMNIST MLP/CNN classifiers with last-hidden widths 64, 128, 256, and 512
evaluations.metric: Training/validation accuracy and last-layer MFR, mean Fano factor, and coefficients of variation
evaluations.result: Ordinary validation accuracy is mostly 88.85%-98.70%; randomized-label training accuracy ranges from 17.31% to 100%. Last-layer randomized-label regimes generally have lower MFR and higher mean Fano factors, with separation changing substantially by width and freezing regime.
evaluations.baseline: Randomly initialized networks and the same architectures trained on true labels

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121 on CIFAR-10 with 64-512-unit ReLU heads
evaluations.result: Ordinary validation accuracy declines from 86.52% to 81.82% as head width increases. Last-layer-only randomized-label conditions show low MFR, whereas all-layer retraining remains much closer to random/generalizing MFR and reaches 100% randomized-label training accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: True-label DenseNet heads, random networks, and alternative layer-freezing conditions

evaluations.setting: Windowed activation-count analysis over all reported networks
evaluations.metric: Mean Fano factor with window size 100
evaluations.result: Most mean Fano factors are below one; randomized-label last-layer-only conditions with very low firing rates approach one. Across Tables 2 and 5 and Figure 6, mean Fano factor is approximately 1-MFR, as expected for binomial counts.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's Poisson reference value F=1

evaluations.setting: Ten epochs on true labels followed by 100 epochs on randomized labels, sampled after each batch
evaluations.metric: Mean firing rate over 100 training/test samples
evaluations.result: Displayed aggregate traces show a sharp MFR drop at each new training regime and later stabilization; all-layer CIFAR-10 retraining is a stated non-stable exception.
evaluations.baseline: MFR immediately before the label-switch transition

evaluations.setting: Exact arXiv v1 PDF and source bundle plus public-code discovery as of 2026-08-24
evaluations.metric: Source identity, page/visual coverage, and executable artifact completeness
evaluations.result: The current arXiv PDF is byte-identical to the pinned 20-page cache and the source archive reproduces the manuscript assets, but no experiment implementation, raw result data, checkpoints, seeds, or dependency lock is released or linked.
evaluations.baseline: An end-to-end artifact that regenerates Tables 1-5 and Figures 2-6

limitations: Author-stated (pp.6, 14): experiments cover only MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 image classification with a small set of MLP, CNN, and DenseNet-based models.
Author-stated (pp.5, 14): only the last hidden layer is observed, although memorization may be distributed across or concentrated in other layers.
Author-stated (pp.8, 14): Fano factors depend on firing rate and window size, and most observed values are below the Poisson reference value.
Author-stated (p.14): randomized labels are a theoretical forced-memorization setting and do not establish behavior for natural overfitting or practical transfer learning.
Reviewer-identified: the finite Bernoulli/binomial observation model explains the headline Fano relationship, invalidating the claimed Poisson-specific interpretation.
Reviewer-identified: several displayed randomized-label models do not fit most labels, confounding memorization with incomplete optimization and model capacity.
Reviewer-identified: seeds, independent-run counts, epoch/stopping details for the main table, shuffle realizations, grid-search space, statistical outputs, and multiplicity accounting are absent.
Reviewer-identified: the KS procedure treats non-rejection as similarity and gives an arithmetically inconsistent Bonferroni threshold, so the no-test-set conclusion lacks equivalence evidence.
Reviewer-identified: ReLU positive rate is sensitive to bias, scaling, normalization, dead units, and optimization state; no matched controls isolate memorization as the causal factor.

Reviewer-identified: no external validation tests threshold choice, alternative activations, natural label noise, modern architectures, larger datasets, calibration, OOD shift, or predictive usefulness on unseen runs.
Reviewer-identified: the public source is manuscript-only, preventing verification of preprocessing, test parameters, raw observations, confidence bands, and table construction.
failure_modes: At moderate activation probabilities, fitting Poisson counts to Bernoulli indicators mechanically produces underdispersion and a spurious Fano-rate relationship.
Very low firing rates make binomial Fano factors approach one, falsely making sparse randomized-label models appear more Poisson-like.
A model that has barely learned randomized labels can be classified as memorizing and drive the same low-rate contrast as a fully fitted memorizer.
Memorization implemented in earlier layers may leave the last-layer statistic unchanged, as suggested by the all-layers DenseNet condition.
Changing biases, normalization, activation functions, preprocessing, or optimizer dynamics can alter zero-threshold firing rates without changing memorization.
Non-rejection in a low-power KS test can be mistaken for proof that training and test activation distributions are equivalent.
ADF and Ljung-Box defaults or aggregation choices can mask binary-series dependence when their settings and outputs are not reported.
Pooling heterogeneous models and datasets can create smooth confidence bands that do not reflect repeatability across random seeds.
An early-stopping trigger based on the label-switch discontinuity may fail under gradual natural overfitting, distribution shift, or ordinary learning-rate transitions.
Without code or raw data, typographical, analytical, and plotting errors cannot be distinguished from implementation behavior.
reusable_insights: Binary activation frequency is a cheap descriptive statistic, but it should be analyzed as Bernoulli/binomial data unless a rare-event limit is justified.
Always plot and derive the null relationship between a dispersion statistic and its estimated rate before treating both as independent diagnostic features.
Memorization diagnostics should stratify by achieved random-label fit and compare checkpoints matched for training loss, parameter distance, and optimization budget.
Layer-local summaries require a layer sweep or causal intervention before conclusions about where memorization resides.
Use equivalence tests or prespecified distance bounds when the desired claim is train/test similarity; ordinary failure to reject is insufficient.
Validate an early-warning score on held-out training runs with lead time, false alarms, sensitivity, and downstream stopping benefit rather than relying on illustrative trajectories.
Release raw per-unit activations and exact scripts because aggregated means and raincloud plots cannot audit dependence tests or uncertainty.
open_questions: Does MFR retain predictive value after controlling for training loss, fraction of randomized labels fitted, dead-ReLU count, bias shifts, architecture, and parameter distance?
Which Bernoulli, beta-binomial, renewal, Markov, or hierarchical count model best describes thresholded activations across shuffled finite datasets?
Can a layerwise rate or entropy profile distinguish naturally overfitted examples from hard-but-generalizable examples without randomized labels?
How stable are activation-rate summaries across seeds, input permutations, thresholds, batch normalization modes, alternative nonlinearities, and realistic distribution shifts?
Can a preregistered MFR-based stopping rule beat validation loss, margin, sharpness, activation-moment, and representation-geometry baselines on held-out model families?
Do causal removal or rewinding experiments show that low-rate units implement memorization, rather than merely correlate with the optimization state?
What changes when activations are modeled jointly across units and layers instead of as independent one-dimensional sequences?

competitive_landscape.title: On the importance of single directions for generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Morcos et al. test reliance on individual activation directions across corrupted-label fractions, hyperparameters, ensembles, and training time and find it predicts generalization. That diagnostic is closer to task reliance and is tested more broadly, whereas Lehmler et al. reduce each unit to a positive frequency and introduce the unsupported Poisson layer.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Meta-Learning Generalization with Activation-Based Early-Stopping
competitive_landscape.difference: Guiroy et al. summarize first and second activation moments across all hidden layers and validate an actual label-free stopping procedure on OOD few-shot tasks. Lehmler et al. offer a simpler scalar tied directly to random-label training, but only suggest early stopping from illustrative trajectories and do not benchmark a decision rule.

competitive_landscape.title: Using Sliced Mutual Information to Study Memorization and Generalization in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Wongso et al. analyze label information in layer features with sliced mutual information, provide theoretical geometric connections, and show layerwise memorization dynamics under label noise. Lehmler et al. are cheaper and label-agnostic at measurement time, but observe only one layer and do not establish a valid probabilistic model.

competitive_landscape.title: On the geometry of generalization and memorization in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Stephenson et al. use replica-based manifold geometry and layer rewinding to argue memorization predominates in deeper layers. Lehmler et al. use that claim to justify observing the last layer, but their all-layer retraining exception and later localization work show why a single aggregate layer cannot identify where memorization occurs.

competitive_landscape.title: Can Neural Network Memorization Be Localized?
competitive_landscape.difference: Maini et al. use gradient accounting, rewinding, retraining, and neuron removal to find memorization in a small set of neurons distributed across layers, directly challenging the final-layer premise. Their interventions address causal localization; Lehmler et al. provide only layer-level correlations from randomized-label states.

competitive_landscape.title: Neuron Activation Coverage: Rethinking Out-of-distribution Detection and Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. combine neuron output with influence on decisions to construct activation coverage, evaluate CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K, and benchmark OOD detection and model selection against 21 methods. Lehmler et al.'s frequency statistic is more minimal, but its evidence is confined to three small benchmarks and forced randomized-label contrasts.

competitive_landscape.title: What do larger image classifiers memorise?
competitive_landscape.difference: Lukasik et al. estimate example-level memorization trajectories across model sizes and show heterogeneous increasing, decreasing, and cap-shaped behavior, including failures of common proxies. That result warns against Lehmler et al.'s aggregate width narrative: a single layer mean can hide opposing example-level trajectories.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first use of stochastic-process models, specifically Poisson arrival processes over thresholded ANN activations, to analyze generalization versus memorization and derive practical firing-rate indicators.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The neuroscience-inspired framing is distinctive, and the descriptive last-layer activation-rate comparison appears incrementally novel relative to activation moments, geometry, and direction-reliance work. The claimed mathematical contribution is not sustained: the actual observation model is Bernoulli/binomial, the reported Fano relation follows algebraically, and several foundational equations and statistical interpretations are incorrect. A later peer-reviewed version appeared as Neurocomputing 598 (2024), article 128473, DOI 10.1016/j.neucom.2024.128473, but the exact pinned arXiv record remains v1. The durable contribution is therefore an exploratory activation-frequency hypothesis, not a validated Poisson framework or general memorization detector.
